extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proofs / introductory discrete mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Solutions and worked guidance for introductory proof and discrete-math exercises (logic, quantifiers, truth tables, combinatorics). Shows how to convert English to symbolic logic, build truth tables, negate quantified statements, and apply counting principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert English sentences into 'If P, then Q' conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Without changing their meanings, convert sentences having constructions like 'provided that', 'necessary', 'only if', 'whenever' into the form 'If P, then Q.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'A matrix is invertible provided that its determinant is not zero.' → 'If a matrix has determinant ≠ 0, then it is invertible.' 'An integer is divisible by 8 only if it is divisible by 4.' → 'If an integer is divisible by 8, then it is divisible by 4.' (Interpret 'but' as 'and' where appropriate; map language cues to antecedent/consequent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert sentences into 'P if and only if Q' for necessary and sufficient conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite statements that assert both necessity and sufficiency in the biconditional 'P if and only if Q' form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'For a matrix to be invertible, it is necessary and sufficient that its determinant is not zero.' → 'A matrix is invertible iff its determinant is not zero.' Use this form when the statement explicitly (or implicitly) asserts both directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write truth tables to evaluate propositions and equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct full truth tables for compound propositions to determine truth values or to test logical equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: list all rows for truth assignments, compute intermediate columns (e.g., Q ⇒ R), then final column. Use examples in text (P ∨ (Q ⇒ R); ∼(P ⇒ Q); (P ∧ ∼P) ∨ Q, etc.). When two formulas have identical final columns, conclude they are logically equivalent ('Since the columns agree...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical equivalences (implication and De Morgan) to transform statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply standard equivalences such as P ⇒ Q = (∼P) ∨ Q and De Morgan's laws ∼(P ∨ Q ∨ R) = (∼P) ∧ (∼Q) ∧ (∼R) to simplify and compare statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples shown: P ⇒ Q = (∼P) ∨ Q; ∼(∼P ∨ ∼Q) = P ∧ Q. Use these equivalences to rewrite conditionals, negate compounds, or reduce to simpler forms before comparing or constructing truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negate quantified statements by swapping quantifiers and negating the predicate
rubrics_metrics.description: To negate statements with ∀ and ∃, swap the quantifiers and place negation on the predicate, working from outermost quantifier inward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Negation of ∀ε > 0 ∃M > 0 (x > M ⇒ |f(x)-b| < ε) becomes ∃ε > 0 ∀M > 0 ∃x (x > M) ∧ ∼(|f(x)-b| < ε). Follow stepwise rewriting: ∼∀ = ∃, ∼∃ = ∀, and negate the inner conditional using its logical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate English statements into symbolic logic with explicit predicates and domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Map English sentences to formal symbolic logic by defining predicates, specifying domains, and using appropriate quantifiers and connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There exists a real a for which a + x = x for every real x.' → ∃a ∈ ℝ ∀x ∈ ℝ, a + x = x. For complex statements, introduce helper predicates/sets (e.g., define R as union of sets) to represent clauses. Note: formal translations emphasize correctness; some nuance/humor may be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret keywords like 'only if', 'provided', 'whenever', 'necessary', 'sufficient' correctly in conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize how common English phrasing maps to antecedent/consequent directions (e.g., 'only if' flips the usual subject→predicate mapping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'A is true only if B' means A ⇒ B. 'A provided that B' means B ⇒ A. 'Whenever' indicates if-then. 'Necessary and sufficient' indicates a biconditional. Apply consistently when converting to formal conditionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the multiplication principle (product rule) for independent choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing sequences or lists where each position has an independent number of choices, multiply counts for each position to get total outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: length-4 lists from 6 letters → 6^4; 8-digit binary strings → 2^8; passwords of length 5 from 52-letter alphabet → 52^5. If a position has restricted choices (first digit cannot be 0), adjust that factor accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the addition principle to count disjoint cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When outcomes are partitioned into disjoint types, add the counts for each type to get the total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of lineups that are all black or all hearts = (#black lineups) + (#hearts lineups); number of password-only-lowercase or only-uppercase = count(lowercase) + count(uppercase). Ensure cases are disjoint or adjust with inclusion-exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the subtraction principle (complement counting) to count 'at least one' or excluded properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the total possibilities and subtract the number of unwanted/complement outcomes to obtain the desired count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: #strings containing at least one 'a' = total − #strings with no 'a'; #integers with repeated digits = total − #integers with no repeated digits. Often simpler than direct counting of the desired property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply permutations P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)! for ordered selections without repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting an ordered sequence of k distinct items from n, use the permutation formula P(n,k) = n(n−1)...(n−k+1) = n!/(n−k)!.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of 7-card lineups from 52 = P(52,7) = 52·51·...·46. Use when order matters and repetition is not allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply combinations C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) for unordered selections without repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting k-element subsets from an n-element set (order doesn't matter), use binomial coefficients C(n,k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of 5-card poker hands from 13 suits, choosing 5 of 13 → C(13,5) = 1287; number of ways to choose positions for ones in a binary string → C(n,k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inclusion-exclusion for unions of overlapping sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Count |A ∪ B ∪ C| by summing individual sizes, subtracting pairwise intersections, and adding triple intersections: |A|+|B|+|C|−|A∩B|−|A∩C|−|B∩C|+|A∩B∩C|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: count 7-digit strings that begin in 1 or end in 1 or have exactly four 1's by computing |A|+|B|+|C| minus pairwise intersections plus triple intersection. Use carefully computed intersections for overlapping properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stars-and-bars method for multisets and distributing identical items
rubrics_metrics.description: Count combinations with repetition or distributions of identical objects into distinct boxes using stars-and-bars: number of k-multisets from n types = C(n+k−1, k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of 10-element multisets from 4 symbols = C(13,10); placing 20 identical balls into 5 boxes = C(24,20); selecting coins with repetition modeled as multisets. Adjust when there are upper bounds by casework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle to force repetition or guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: If n items are placed into m boxes with n > m, at least one box contains ≥⌈n/m⌉ items; use to guarantee repeated residues or repeated outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: choose 6 integers → two share same remainder mod 5 (6 items into 5 boxes). To guarantee 10 occurrences of the same dice face, solve for smallest n with ⌈n/6⌉ ≥ 10 → n = 55.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutations with repeated elements (multinomial / division by factorials)
rubrics_metrics.description: For arrangements of n objects with repeated types (counts a,b,...), use n!/(a! b! ...) to account for indistinguishable permutations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'TENNESSEE' (9 letters with repeats 4!,2!,2! etc.) → number of distinct permutations = 9!/(4!2!2!1!). Use Fact 3.8 style formula for words with repeated letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting with positional constraints (first digit nonzero, last digit even, fixed positions)
rubrics_metrics.description: When some positions are constrained, treat those positions with adjusted choice counts and apply multiplication/addition/subtraction as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: count even 4-digit numbers (first digit 1–9, last digit even) using 9·10·10·5; count binary strings that begin or end with 1 by fixing those positions (2^9 or 2^8 factors) and applying inclusion-exclusion for overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casework: partition problem into types and sum counts
rubrics_metrics.description: When outcomes naturally divide into a small number of types (positions of vowels, where consecutive vowels appear, etc.), compute count for each type via multiplication then add results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: lists with two consecutive vowels in length-6 lists: consider placements V V * * * *, *V V * * * etc.; compute each type's count and add (here each type had equal count 720 leading to 5·720=3600).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial (double-counting) proofs for identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove combinatorial identities by counting the same set two ways (e.g., count 3-element subsets of S by fixing a middle element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: show sum_{k=1}^n k(n+1−k) = C(n+2,3) by counting 3-element subsets {j,k,ℓ} with fixed middle k: there are k(n+1−k) choices for each k; summing over k gives total C(n+2,3). Use 'count same objects different ways' technique for identities like C(n,k) relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the binomial theorem and properties of binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the binomial theorem to compute coefficients and to derive combinatorial identities/sums of binomial coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: coefficient of x^8 in (x+2)^13 found via C(13,5)·2^5; sums like Σ C(n,k) = 2^n from (1+1)^n; alternating sums using (1+(−1))^n = 0. Use substitution in (x+y)^n to derive various identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat English connectives carefully (e.g., 'but' as 'and') when negating or translating
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify colloquial connectives: 'but' can be treated logically as conjunction when negating or translating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The number x is positive, but the number y is not positive.' → interpret as x positive ∧ y not positive; its negation is 'x not positive or y positive' via De Morgan's law. Avoid over-literal colloquial readings that alter logical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use logical reasoning (not brute-force) when possible to deduce truth values
rubrics_metrics.description: Some truth-value deductions can be made without constructing full truth tables by reasoning about implications and falsity/ truth of components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Given P false and (R ⇒ S) ⇔ (P ∧ Q) true, deduce P∧Q false so R⇒S must be false, hence R true and S false. Use logical relationships to shortcut full-table computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When counting outcomes with multiple restrictions, split into manageable subcases (e.g., last digit zero vs not zero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break intersection counts into subparts based on a critical position or condition to compute intersections accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: computing |A ∩ B| for even 7-digit numbers with exactly three zeros: split into cases depending on whether the last digit is 0 or not, compute each using multiplication and stars-and-bars, then sum.
